entries.topic: Mangal Dosha is not marriage doom

copy.headline: Mangal Dosha won't ruin your marriage.
copy.body:
Mangal Dosha simply means Mars sits in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th or 12th house from your lagna. Those houses touch self, family, home, partnership, longevity and loss — so classical authors flagged Mars there as heat applied to relationship territory. That is the entire mechanism.

The same texts list cancellations most people never hear about: Mars in its own signs (Aries, Scorpio), exalted in Capricorn, or both partners carrying the placement. A large share of 'manglik' charts are neutralised by the very rules that define the dosha.

One placement never decides a marriage — it describes an intensity to understand, not a sentence to fear.
copy.factor_line: Mars in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th or 12th house from the lagna — that placement, and nothing else, is Mangal Dosha.

copy.headline: Your 8th house isn't scary. It's about depth.
copy.body:
The 8th house got branded the 'house of death' and never lived it down. In practice it governs what transforms you: shared resources, inheritance, intimacy, research, the psyche's basement.

The structure explains the reputation. The 8th sits opposite your 2nd house of personal wealth — it is what you hold jointly with others, and what you cannot control alone. That loss of sole control is the real theme, and it's why the house feels intense rather than evil.

A strong 8th shows up in surgeons, analysts, therapists and researchers — people who go beneath the surface for a living.
copy.factor_line: The 8th house is the 2nd from the 7th — your partner's resources and everything held jointly — which is why it rules both intimacy and inheritance.
copy.caption:
You've been told the 8th house means death. Here's what it actually governs.

In Jyotish the 8th house rules transformation: joint assets, inheritance, intimacy, research, and the parts of life you can't control alone. The 'death' label comes from it marking endings — but every ending it marks is paired with what comes after.

The structure shows its work: the 8th is the 2nd house counted from the 7th, so it literally describes your partner's resources and everything you hold jointly. That's why one house covers marriage finances, deep bonds and inheritance at the same time.

Houses describe themes, not verdicts — an occupied 8th house reads as depth to work with, never a doom flag.

copy.headline: What is a nakshatra?
copy.body:
A nakshatra is one of 27 lunar mansions — equal 13°20′ segments of the sidereal zodiac that the Moon crosses at a rate of roughly one per day.

Your janma nakshatra is simply the segment the Moon occupied at your birth, computed from its exact sidereal longitude. It seeds your Vimshottari dasha sequence, colours your Moon sign, and drives most muhurat and matching calculations.

27 mansions × 13°20′ covers the full 360° — one of the oldest coordinate systems in Indian astronomy, older than the 12-sign zodiac itself.
copy.factor_line: 27 equal segments of 13°20′ each, measured along the Moon's sidereal path — your nakshatra is a coordinate, not a vibe.
copy.caption:
You know your sign. Do you know your nakshatra? It does far more work in your kundli.

A nakshatra is one of 27 lunar mansions — equal slices of 13°20′ along the sidereal zodiac. The Moon crosses about one per day, and your janma nakshatra is whichever slice it occupied at your birth, computed from the Moon's exact longitude.

Why it matters: the nakshatra — not the sign — starts your Vimshottari dasha clock, refines your Moon-sign reading, and sits underneath almost every muhurat and matching calculation. It's the fine grain of the whole system.

The positions are astronomy; the meanings layered on them are interpretation — precise inputs, human readings.

entries.topic: The birth-time setting NRIs get wrong

copy.headline: Born in India, living abroad? Your chart may be set to the wrong clock.
copy.body:
The most common NRI chart error isn't the birth time — it's the timezone. Apps quietly default to your current location, so a 7:15 AM Chennai birth gets read as 7:15 AM New Jersey.

The lagna advances about 1° every 4 minutes and changes sign roughly every 2 hours. A timezone slip of hours doesn't nudge your chart — it hands you a different lagna, different house lords, a different dasha start.

The fix is simple: always enter the birthplace and the local time at birth (IST for India), and let the software do the conversion.
copy.factor_line: The lagna moves ~1° every 4 minutes; a timezone mix-up of even 30 minutes can shift every house in the chart.
copy.caption:
You've been told your chart 'doesn't feel like you'. Check the timezone before you blame the stars.

The single most common mistake we see from NRIs: entering an India birth time while the app assumes your current city's timezone. The chart gets cast for the wrong sky entirely — a 7:15 AM Chennai birth read as 7:15 AM in New Jersey is nine and a half hours off.

Why it matters mechanically: the ascendant (lagna) advances about one degree every four minutes and changes sign every two hours or so. Get the zone wrong by a few hours and you don't get a slightly-off chart — you get someone else's lagna, house layout and dasha timeline.

A chart is an interpretation built on one precise input — the moment and place of birth. Give it the right input.

entries.topic: Sade Sati — what Saturn's 7.5 years actually are

copy.headline: Sade Sati is not a 7.5-year curse.
copy.body:
Sade Sati is Saturn's transit through the 12th, 1st and 2nd signs from your natal Moon — roughly 2.5 years per sign, 7.5 in total. That adjacency to the Moon is the entire definition.

The three phases carry different themes — release, pressure, rebuilding — and the intensity is chart-specific: it depends on Saturn's sign, house and dignity in your own kundli, not on a one-size-fits-all script.

Saturn returns every ~29 years, so Sade Sati is a recurring season most people meet two or three times — not a once-in-a-lifetime sentence.

entries.topic: Rashi vs sun sign — different planet, different zodiac

copy.headline: 'But I'm a Leo…' — your kundli may disagree.
copy.body:
Your Western 'sign' is where the Sun sat in the tropical zodiac, which is tied to the seasons. Your rashi is where the Moon sat in the sidereal zodiac, which is tied to the actual stars.

That's two differences at once: a different planet (Moon vs Sun) and a different zodiac. The sidereal frame currently trails the tropical one by about 24° — the ayanamsa — enough to move most people's Sun back a sign, while the Moon is somewhere else entirely.

So 'I'm a Leo' and 'my rashi is Karka' can both be true. They're answers to different questions.
copy.factor_line: Rashi = the Moon's sidereal sign; sun sign = the Sun's tropical sign — different planet, different zodiac, offset by the ~24° ayanamsa.
copy.caption:
You've called yourself a Leo your whole life. Your kundli might quietly disagree — and both can be right.

Western sun signs use the tropical zodiac, anchored to the equinoxes. Jyotish uses the sidereal zodiac, anchored to the stars — and its headline sign is your rashi: the Moon's sign, not the Sun's. The two zodiacs are offset by the ayanamsa, currently about 24 degrees.

That offset alone shifts most people's Sun back one sign when they move between systems — and the rashi, being the Moon, follows a completely different rhythm anyway (the Moon changes sign roughly every 2.25 days, the Sun once a month).

Neither system is 'wrong' — they're different coordinate frames, and everything read from either one is interpretation, not physics.

entries.topic: What is Kaal Sarp Dosha, honestly?

copy.headline: What is Kaal Sarp Dosha, honestly?
copy.body:
Kaal Sarp Dosha is the condition where all seven classical planets sit within the arc between Rahu and Ketu — the Moon's nodes — hemming the whole chart onto one side.

The honest part: it does not appear in the core classical texts like Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra. It's a comparatively modern formulation, and traditions differ on whether it matters at all.

If your chart has it, it's worth a careful reading of Rahu and Ketu by house and sign — not a payment plan for fear-based remedies.
copy.factor_line: All seven grahas placed within the Rahu–Ketu axis — one geometric condition, absent from the earliest classical texts.
copy.caption:
You've been told Kaal Sarp Dosha explains everything going wrong. Here's the honest version.

The definition is geometric: all seven classical planets fall on one side of the Rahu–Ketu axis. That's the entire condition — and it's common enough that a meaningful share of all charts qualify on any given definition.

What the fear-merchants skip: Kaal Sarp Dosha isn't described in foundational texts like Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra. It's a later, popular construct — which is exactly why interpretations of it vary so wildly, and why it should never be sold to you as a certified emergency.

If your chart shows it, read Rahu and Ketu by house and sign like any other placement — interpretation, not diagnosis.

entries.topic: DST and your birth chart — a 1-hour error changes the lagna

copy.headline: A 1-hour DST error can change your lagna.
copy.body:
If you were born abroad — or your family recorded a clock time during a daylight-saving period — your chart may be cast an hour off without anyone noticing.

The lagna changes sign roughly every two hours, so a one-hour error shifts it by about 15° — often enough to tip it into the next sign. New lagna, new house lords, new dasha timing: effectively a different chart.

India has DST traps too: 'war time' was observed from 1942 to 1945, so charts from those years need the correction. Good software checks the historical timezone database — always confirm yours did.
copy.factor_line: The ascendant advances ~15° per hour — one unaccounted DST hour can move every house cusp and often the lagna sign itself.
copy.caption:
You've double-checked your birth time. Did anyone check the clock it was read from?

Daylight saving is the quietest chart-breaker there is. A birth recorded at 6:30 during DST was really 5:30 standard time — and since the lagna moves through a full sign about every two hours, that missing hour shifts it roughly 15 degrees, frequently into a different sign altogether.

A different lagna means different house rulers and a different dasha timeline — not a small rounding error but a structurally different chart. This bites NRIs born in Europe and North America most, and even India observed war-time DST from 1942 to 1945.

A chart is only as honest as its input — verify the timezone rules for your birth date and place before trusting any reading.

copy.headline: The 'marriage chart' isn't a second horoscope.
copy.body:
The navamsa (D9) divides each sign into nine parts of 3°20′ and re-plots every planet by that division — a second chart derived entirely from the first.

3°20′ is exactly one nakshatra pada, so D9 is your chart read at nakshatra-quarter resolution. Classically it answers two questions: how strong a planet really is beneath its rashi placement, and how the marriage-and-partnership axis holds up.

It refines the birth chart; it never replaces it.

copy.headline: What is a tithi?
copy.body:
A tithi is a lunar day: the time the Moon takes to move 12° further from the Sun. Thirty tithis make one lunar month — fifteen waxing (shukla paksha) toward purnima, fifteen waning (krishna paksha) toward amavasya.

Because the Moon's speed varies along its orbit, a tithi can run anywhere from about 19 to 26 hours — which is why festival dates wander across the solar calendar.

The tithi is the first limb of the panchang and the backbone of muhurat selection.
copy.factor_line: One tithi = 12° of Moon–Sun angular separation — pure geometry, which is why its length varies from day to day.
copy.caption:
Ever wondered why Diwali moves around the calendar? The tithi is why.

A tithi is a lunar day — each 12° the Moon pulls ahead of the Sun. Thirty of them make a lunar month: fifteen brightening toward purnima, fifteen fading toward amavasya. And since the Moon speeds up and slows down along its orbit, tithis stretch and shrink between roughly 19 and 26 hours.

Festivals, fasts and muhurats are all fixed by tithi, not by the solar date — so the 'moving' festival is actually the most precisely defined one on your calendar.

Panchang elements are astronomy first, interpretation second — the angle is exact even when the meaning is traditional.

copy.headline: What is a lagna?
copy.body:
The lagna (ascendant) is the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the exact moment and place of your birth. It anchors the whole chart: the lagna becomes your 1st house, and every other house counts from it.

It moves fast — through all twelve signs every day, roughly one sign every two hours — which is why birth time matters more for the lagna than for anything else in your kundli.

Sun sign, Moon sign, lagna: three different anchors. Jyotish reads all three, but the houses hang off the lagna.
copy.factor_line: The lagna is the eastern-horizon sign at the birth moment — it fixes the 1st house, so a two-hour clock error re-numbers your entire chart.
copy.caption:
You know your sun sign. You maybe know your rashi. The chart is actually built on a third thing.

The lagna, or ascendant, is whichever sign was rising in the east at your exact birth moment and place. It becomes house number one, and all twelve houses count from there — so it decides which planet rules your chart and where every life theme lands.

Because the Earth turns through the whole zodiac daily, the lagna changes sign about every two hours. That's why serious Jyotish is obsessive about birth time: the Sun barely moves in a day, the Moon a little, but the lagna is sprinting.

The houses are a frame for interpretation, not a verdict — but the frame has to be set from the right moment.

copy.headline: What is guna milan?
copy.body:
Guna milan is the traditional compatibility score: two Moon charts compared across eight kootas worth 1 to 8 points each, 36 in total.

Everything is computed from just two data points per person — the Moon's sign and the Moon's nakshatra. Temperament, influence, rhythm, instinct, emotional friendship, nature, sign distance, constitution: each koota tests one dimension.

18 is the customary pass mark, but the two heaviest kootas (Nadi and Bhakoot) come with classical cancellation rules — so the raw number is a starting point, never the verdict.
copy.factor_line: Eight kootas scored from each partner's Moon nakshatra and Moon sign — 36 points of Moon-chart comparison, nothing more, nothing less.
copy.caption:
'We scored 22 out of 36.' Out of what, exactly? Here's what guna milan measures.

It's a comparison of two Moon charts across eight kootas — Varna, Vashya, Tara, Yoni, Graha Maitri, Gana, Bhakoot, Nadi — worth 1 through 8 points. Every point comes from just the Moon's sign and nakshatra in each chart.

The heavyweights, Nadi (8) and Bhakoot (7), also carry classical exceptions that can flip a 'fail' into a pass — exceptions most instant calculators never apply. Tradition treats 18-plus as workable, but the texts themselves treat the score as one input among many.

Compatibility scoring is a centuries-old heuristic, not a measurement — let it inform the conversation, not replace it.
